authors: Robert Chansler; Hairong Kuang; Sanjay Radia; Konstantin Shvachko; Suresh Srinivas
problem: A metadata service records a directory mutation and returns success to its client.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The historical HDFS chapter distinguishes journal synchronization from acknowledgement.
tradeoffs: Storage synchronization can increase write latency; batching amortizes that work.

problem: A message relay receives bursts faster than its network connection can drain them.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: Queued messages contribute latency; an unbounded queue can make latency unbounded.
tradeoffs: Batching can raise throughput while adding delay for individual messages.

problem: A financial-import worker increments an account's monthly spending total, then crashes before acknowledging delivery.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The Mint exercise describes periodic extraction and categorization of transactions.
tradeoffs: The exercise's workload assumptions are illustrative and do not establish a production guarantee.

problem: A fan-out worker writes a timeline entry and invokes a push-notification provider; queue delivery can repeat.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The Twitter exercise separates tweet ingestion, fan-out, and timeline retrieval.
tradeoffs: Fan-out work depends on follower distribution, not just the average recipient count.

problem: A messaging API writes accepted messages to a leader before replying; the requirement includes loss of that host.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The scaling exercise introduces additional database instances and replication as traffic grows.
tradeoffs: Replica count alone does not specify synchronous acknowledgement or failover safety.

problem: A metric collector accepts points into a pending-write buffer while its disk writer is temporarily slow.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The Graphite chapter discusses buffering writes to work around storage throughput limits.
tradeoffs: Buffered acceptance and durable persistence must be distinguished for a loss-sensitive workload.

problem: A replayable sales event increments a product's ranking counter; retries can arrive up to two days later.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The sales-rank exercise uses sales data to compute product rankings.
tradeoffs: Aggregation and retry policy need explicit semantics when records can be replayed.

authors: Francesco Cesarini; Andy Gross; Justin Sheehy
problem: A replicated message store acknowledges an accepted message; users require survival of a full host loss.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The Riak account describes replication and fault tolerance in a distributed key-value store.
tradeoffs: A system family name does not establish a particular deployment's durability settings.

problem: An asynchronous image-message pipeline accumulates work during a sustained traffic spike.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The distributed web architecture chapter explains asynchronous queues and scaling trade-offs.
tradeoffs: A queue can absorb a temporary burst; it cannot resolve a permanent arrival-rate deficit.

problem: An API reports that a text message has been accepted and must remain available after a process crash.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The pastebin exercise separates writes, content storage, and reads.
tradeoffs: Storage sizing assumptions are distinct from the acknowledgement contract.

problem: A crawler-result worker charges a per-page processing counter; a timed-out task may be redelivered.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The crawler exercise considers distributing URL fetching and processing work.
tradeoffs: Revisiting a URL can be intentional; a retry identity must distinguish it from a new crawl task.

problem: A gateway fronts a slow message-processing service while concurrent requests rise.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The nginx account explains event-driven handling of concurrent connections.
tradeoffs: Efficient connection handling does not itself establish downstream queue capacity.

problem: A wiki edit triggers a queued notification and an external mail-provider call that may be replayed.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The MediaWiki account discusses decomposing web requests and deferred work.
tradeoffs: An internal database guard does not automatically cover an external notification provider.

problem: A message service persists an accepted operation using a storage system with configurable durability.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The NoSQL overview discusses differing storage and consistency design choices.
tradeoffs: Product categories alone do not specify persistence or acknowledgement guarantees.

problem: A social-graph mutation queue buffers accepted relationship updates while the graph store is unavailable.
conditions: Use the historical text as background; evaluate only explicit facts of the new design.
lesson: The social-graph exercise describes storage and access patterns for relationships.
tradeoffs: Graph connectivity and traffic skew change resource demand; acceptance must still have a clear contract.
